text: Six children look over a wall at a beach.
From up here they can see all of it at once. They cannot touch any of it.
On the sand there is no view of the whole. There is a ball, cold water, and whatever happens next. Here they can change things.
Later they climb back up and look again. The beach is empty.
The day is still with them, but not as a film. It is a handful of bright moments, and each time they tell it they join the dots a little differently.
They can look at the day now. They cannot kick the ball.
Kierkegaard put it in two sentences. Life must be understood backwards. It must be lived forwards.
There is a danger in looking back. Suppose a learner did nothing but rehearse its own day, over and over.
Its score on that day climbs until it is perfect. Its grasp of new days gets worse. In the end it knows less than if it had learned nothing.
A measure, once it becomes the only target, stops measuring. That is called Goodhart's law.
So what happens at night? One idea is that dreams take the dots and jumble them. The ball rolls uphill. The sea is in the wrong place.
A learner that practises on jumbled days never gets a perfect score. It stays ready for a day it has not seen.
That is a hypothesis, not a finding. The arithmetic behind it is sound.
In the morning the children go back to the wall. The beach is there, and it is not yesterday's.
